extracted.intended_audience: researchers and contributors working on automated theorem proving / formalization (authors of formal statements/proofs for the miniF2F benchmark)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing, naming, formatting, licensing, and contributing formalized problem statements and example proofs to the MiniF2F benchmark across multiple formal systems (Lean, Metamath, HOL Light, Isabelle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark composition / source material
rubrics_metrics.description: MiniF2F is a formal mathematics benchmark consisting of exercise statements from olympiads (AMC, AIME, IMO) as well as high-school and undergraduate maths classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to provide a shared benchmark to evaluate and directly compare automated theorem proving systems based on the formal systems targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem representation minimum content
rubrics_metrics.description: Each problem is represented by a unique name and a file for each of the formal systems we target. Each file consists at minima in the problem statement and optionally one or more example proofs associated with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Files should include at least the problem statement; example proofs and supporting lemmas are optional but encouraged to provide ground-truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset splits and intended use
rubrics_metrics.description: The benchmark is divided in two splits: valid and test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: valid: validation set that can be used while designing automated theorem proving systems (early-stopping, reinforcement learning, data-augmentation, curriculum design, ...). test: held-out test set reserved for final evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming conventions for problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Olympiads problems are generally named after their competition year and problem number (eg. imo-1990-p3 or aime-1983-p2). Problems coming from a particular dataset are named to ease retrieval (eg. mathd-algebra-125). Other problems are prefixed by a category hint and a unique name in the style of Metamath naming conventions (eg. induction-11div10tonmn1ton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming conventions are still a work in progress; choose names that make retrieval easy and follow existing patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean: aggregation of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Since having one file per statement causes slowness in Lean parsing stage, all Lean statements are exceptionally aggregated in two files (valid.lean and test.lean). These files contain a list of the problem statements defined as theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use valid.lean and test.lean to hold statements; do not create one file per statement for Lean unless there is a compelling reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean: statement vs lemma rule
rubrics_metrics.description: No theorem should appear that do not correspond to a problem statement; use lemma instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem statements must be declared with theorem. Any auxiliary results that are not problem statements should be declared as lemma to avoid confusion with benchmark items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean: linter and formatter requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Please use lean/scripts/lint_style.py to check all the statements pass the linter. You can also make use of lean/scripts/simple_formatter.sh to enforce a few basic formatting rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run the linter and formatter prior to submitting contributions to ensure consistent style and reduce CI/style-related review comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean: installation and build steps
rubrics_metrics.description: To install the project make sure you have elan installed, then in the directory where you want the project installed run: git clone https://github.com/openai/miniF2F; cd miniF2F; leanpkg configure; leanpkg build.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these procedural steps to set up the Lean environment and build the aggregated statement files locally before contributing or testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath file convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Each file contains the problem statement with the same name as the problem unique name. The statement is commented (using Metamath convention) if provided without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure filename matches the unique problem name; if there is no proof include the statement as a comment according to Metamath conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: HOL Light file convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Each file contains the problem statement defined as a HOL Light term whose name must match the file name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name the HOL Light term to exactly match the file name to avoid mismatches and to allow automated tooling to locate statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isabelle file convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Each file contains the problem statement defined as a theorem whose name must match the file name, optionally with a proof for it as well as the necessary imports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include necessary imports for Isabelle files; name the theorem to match the filename; proofs are optional but encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: License per formal-system folder
rubrics_metrics.description: The lean folder is released under the Apache License (so that it is aligned with Lean's mathlib license). The metamath folder is released under the MIT License. The hollight folder is released under the FreeBSD License. The isabelle folder is released under the Apache License.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the indicated licenses when contributing code or proofs to the corresponding folders; the benchmark is released under permissive licenses overall (MIT for Metamath, Apache for Lean).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versioning and reporting policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A version of miniF2F is defined by a frozen set of statements. When reporting a result based on miniF2F please always specify the version you used. Each version will live in its own branch to allow later additions of translated statements or fixes to existing statements as needed. The main branch remains reserved for active development and should not be used when reporting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the versioned branches (e.g., v1) for reproducible evaluations and include the version identifier in publications and result reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active version info expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The current version is v1, frozen as of August 2021, including 244 statements (fully translated to Lean and Metamath but still WIP in other formal systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the current coverage per system for the version you use; do not assume all systems have full translations unless stated for that version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions encouraged and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: All contributions, such as new statements for later versions, addition of missing statements for existing versions, bug fixes, additional proofs are all welcome. If you're using it and discovering new proofs (manually or automatically) please contribute them back to the benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contribute via pull requests; the benchmark is intended as a shared resource for the machine learning and formalization communities and contributions improve coverage and ground-truth proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal for version coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal for each version is to get full coverage on all formal systems for that version even if that might not be the case when the version is frozen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When curating or contributing, prioritize achieving translations and proofs across all targeted formal systems to maximize cross-system comparability.
